Large-codebase maintainability is only implied, and community users who built semi-large or complex apps report data-flow and 'magic' friction, though these are preferences rather than concrete failures. Missing for 10: first-party guidance or benchmarks showing sustained performance at large-app scale, documented team-scale maintainability practices (community notes there are no accepted best practices), and independent evidence of large codebases staying fast and maintainable over time.

rationale: The vuejs/core repo maintains a public GitHub Security Advisories page with private vulnerability reporting and at least one published advisory, a High-severity SSR XSS (GHSA-g2v6-rqmx-r4w6) with publisher and date. rationale: Vue's official Suspense guide documents a built-in <Suspense> component that renders a loading state through #fallback slots while nested async setup() and async components resolve. That covers the suspense half of the story. However, Vue flags <Suspense> as experimental with an API that may change, and the evidence shows no dedicated resource primitive that turns server-loaded data into reactive state. missing for 10: a documented resource/data-loading primitive that exposes fetched data as reactive state, stable (non-experimental) Suspense status, independent hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a developer, I can treat server-loaded data as reactive state and build a responsive loading UI for it using resource and suspense primitives

citations.quote: <Suspense> is a built-in component for orchestrating async dependencies in a component tree. It can render a loading state while waiting for multiple nested async dependencies down the component tree to be resolved.
<Suspense> is an experimental feature. It is not guaranteed to reach stable status and the API may change before it does.

rationale: Vue's official SSR API documents several streaming renderers in vue/server-renderer: Node.js Readable streams, Web ReadableStream, pipe-to-writable variants and renderToSimpleStream. These work in both Node and edge environments such as Cloudflare Workers. Vue 3.5+ also adds lazy hydration strategies that let async components hydrate on idle, on visibility or on interaction, which serves the 'reach interactivity faster' goal. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that streaming SSR works well in practice.

support.subject: As a developer, I can render my application on the server with streaming support to reach interactivity faster

rationale: Vue's official SSR API reference documents first-party streaming renderers in vue/server-renderer for Node streams and Web Streams, so server HTML can be sent progressively. The lazy hydration strategies added in 3.5 let that content display before client code hydrates it. A 2017 community comment naming streaming SSR as a React advantage is old general preference, not a concrete failure, so it does not create a dispute. rationale: Vue's official TypeScript docs say the defineProps() macro in <script setup> infers prop types from the runtime declaration with no extra annotations, which covers the props half of the story. For emitted events, the docs only say emits 'can also be typed' via runtime or type declaration, which does not clearly show annotation-free inference. A hands-on community report says complex props still need manual PropType casts; this narrows the claim rather than refuting it. missing for 10: explicit documentation that emitted-event payload types are inferred automatically without annotations, evidence that inference covers complex/object prop types without PropType casts, independent corroboration of the inference behavior.

support.subject: As a developer, I can get automatic type inference for component props and emitted events without writing extra type annotations

citations.quote: When using <script setup>, the defineProps() macro supports inferring the props types based on its argument

rationale: The evidence pack documents TypeScript inference only inside script blocks: defineProps and emit typing in <script setup>. Nothing shows compile-time type checking of template expressions; the 'Tooling Guide' entry is a bare title with no content. Template type checking is a fair axis for a UI framework, so the absence of evidence yields 'none', not 'na'.

support.subject: As a developer, I can get compile-time type checking inside my component templates, not just script blocks

rationale: Vue's releases page has a TypeScript Definitions policy. It warns that type definitions may break between minor versions and that Vue may raise the minimum required TypeScript version. It also recommends locking the Vue minor version to avoid breaks. However, the evidence never states which TypeScript versions are actually supported. Missing for 10: an explicit list of supported or minimum TypeScript versions, a per-Vue-release compatibility matrix, and independent corroboration.

support.subject: As a developer, I know which TypeScript versions the framework officially supports so I can avoid compatibility breaks when upgrading either one

citations.quote: Occasionally we may need to adopt features that are only available in a newer version of TypeScript, raising the minimum required version of TypeScript.

rationale: Vue's official docs list a first-party "Migration from Vue 2" guide, so an official upgrade path exists for the major version jump. The release policy adds that deprecated features keep working until the next major release, and TypeScript users should upgrade manually when a new minor ships. The guide appears only as a navigation title, though, so its depth and step-by-step content are unproven. Missing for 10: evidence of the guide's actual content (breaking-change lists, migration build or codemods, step-by-step instructions), upgrade guidance for minor versions, and hands-on corroboration that developers followed it successfully.

rationale: Vue's official guide documents defineCustomElement. It builds standards-based custom elements from the same component APIs as defineComponent and returns a constructor that extends HTMLElement. The guide also covers customElements.define registration, shadow-root styles, SFC-based custom elements and shipping component libraries as custom elements. missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration of authoring custom elements with Vue.

support.subject: As a developer, I can author standards-based web components and custom elements using the framework

citations.quote: Vue supports creating custom elements using exactly the same Vue component APIs via the defineCustomElement method. The method accepts the same argument as defineComponent, but instead returns a custom element constructor that extends HTMLElement.
